title: Discrete distributions and statistical mechanics of small systems
abstract: We study connections between discrete probability distributions and the statistical mechanics of small systems. Using probability generating functions, we develop the theory of power series, infinitely divisible, and scalable distributions of non-negative integer-valued random variables, and introduce the class of Markovian distributions that arise naturally in stationary solutions of birth-death processes and in scalable infinitely divisible distributions.   These results are applied to the grand canonical ensemble description in statistical mechanics: the infinite divisibility leads to a quasiparticle picture of an interacting gas, and the virial expansion is linked to the combinants of the distribution. A kinetic model of the liquid-vapor phase transition is presented, in which the particle-number distribution at the critical point converges to the Discrete Stable distribution - the fixed point of a renormalization semi-group transformation. We also show that the scalability of the particle-number distribution is preserved in Tsallis non-extensive thermodynamics, even though infinite divisibility fails. Moreover, deformed discrete distributions, including the negative binomial as a q-deformation of the Poisson, arise naturally in this setting.
summary: This work develops a theoretical framework linking advanced concepts in discrete probability distributions—such as infinite divisibility and scalability—to the statistical mechanics of small systems. By applying these mathematical tools, the authors model phase transitions and derive equations of state for interacting gases. It provides a powerful combinatorial approach to understanding critical phenomena beyond standard assumptions.
main_problem: The paper investigates the mathematical connections between discrete probability distributions and the statistical mechanics description of small, interacting systems.
main_result: It establishes that the particle-number distribution at a critical point converges to the Discrete Stable distribution, and it extends these concepts to non-extensive thermodynamics while maintaining scalability properties.
method: The analysis heavily relies on probability generating functions (p.g.f.) to develop theories for infinitely divisible and scalable distributions, applying these tools within the grand canonical ensemble framework.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the particle-number distribution $p_k$ in small systems, modeling phenomena like liquid-vapor phase transitions using kinetic models and analyzing equations of state (e.g., van der Waals).
key_observables: Particle-number distribution ($p_k$), Equation of State ($ eta p$ vs $ho$), Virial coefficients, and the Discrete Stable distribution.
important_parameters: Critical point parameters ($ho_c, T_c$), temperature ratios ($	au = T/T_c$), and non-extensivity parameter $q$.
main_assumptions: The analysis often assumes infinite divisibility in the grand canonical ensemble, though it also explores regimes where this fails (e.g., Tsallis thermodynamics).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from developing general mathematical tools using p.g.f.s for discrete distributions to applying these tools to construct equations of state and analyze phase transitions in statistical mechanics.
why_interesting: While the focus is on classical statistical mechanics, the rigorous mathematical treatment of distribution properties (like infinite divisibility and scaling) has deep parallels with quantum many-body theories involving correlation functions or reduced density matrices.
